assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Mobile phase
items.clue: The part that moves: the solvent.

items.label: Stationary phase
items.clue: The part that does not move: the paper.

items.label: Origin (baseline)
items.clue: The pencil line on which the samples are spotted.

items.label: Solvent front
items.clue: The furthest point the liquid reaches up the paper.

questions.stem: In the chemical sense of the word, which of these samples is pure?

options.text: Distilled water, which contains only the compound H2O
Sea water, because it is clear and colourless
Spring water bottled with nothing added at all
Clean air, since each of the gases in it is pure

questions.explanation: A pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance, and distilled water is only H2O.

questions.stem: A student says carbon dioxide must be a mixture because it contains two different elements. Why is the student wrong?

options.text: It is a colourless gas, and colourless gases are pure
Carbon and oxygen are pure, so this gas is pure
Its atoms are chemically bonded in fixed proportions
Its elements are only mixed, not chemically bonded

questions.explanation: A pure substance is a single element or compound, and in a compound the elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions.

questions.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that a solid sample is pure?

options.text: It melts gradually over a range of several degrees
It melts sharply at one specific temperature
It is a fine white powder with no visible specks
It melts at a temperature well over 100 °C

questions.explanation: Pure elements and compounds melt at specific temperatures, so a sharp melting point is the evidence wanted.

questions.stem: A sample of sea water starts to boil at 102 °C and the temperature keeps rising while it boils. What does this show?

options.text: Salt gives the water a new fixed boiling point
The water in it is a different compound
It is pure, since nothing was added to it
It is a mixture, not a pure substance

questions.explanation: Boiling over a range rather than at one specific temperature is how boiling point data reveal a mixture.

questions.stem: A carton of milk is labelled pure milk. What does the word pure mean on that label?

options.text: It holds only one compound, so it is chemically pure
Nothing has been added to it, so it is in its natural state
It has been filtered until only water and fat are left
Every part of it looks the same, so it is one substance

questions.explanation: In everyday language a pure substance is one that is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.

questions.stem: Pure aspirin melts at 135 °C. A student's prepared sample melts between 122 °C and 128 °C. What do the data show?

options.text: It is pure aspirin, since the average is close to the book value
It is pure, because pure solids melt over a range of degrees
It is impure, because an impurity raises the melting point
It is impure: the impurity lowered and spread the melting point

questions.explanation: An impurity lowers a melting point and spreads it over a range, which is what these data show.

questions.stem: Four liquids were heated to boiling. Which behaviour identifies a pure liquid?

options.text: It boils steadily at 78 °C until it has all gone
It boils at 100 °C and leaves a white solid behind
It boils away over a range from 78 °C to 91 °C
It starts to boil at 95 °C and the temperature rises

questions.explanation: A pure compound boils at a specific temperature, which stays constant throughout boiling.
